name: Vertical football
scopeNote: Vertical football / transition-first: win the ball (often by counter-pressing), then play it forward at once and sprint into space instead of building through midfield. The only tier-B+ source here is Michael Cox (Sky Sports): Dortmund 2011/12 were 'perfectly solid without possession' and defending deep suited their counter-attacking; Bleacher Report says BVB 'always look for the opportunity to counterattack, playing the ball forward immediately'. Exemplar: Dortmund under Klopp (team file dortmund-2010-13, 2010-08-14 to 2013-05-25, includes the 2010/11 title that Hard Tackle covers; the focus is 2011-13). No source in this run uses the exact label 'vertical football'; sources say 'direct', 'counterattack', 'transitions', 'one-dimensional'. Kept distinct from gegenpressing (the press-after-loss mechanism, gegenpressing.json), heavy-metal-football (Klopp's tempo/attitude brand, mainly Liverpool 2018-20) and red-bull-school (Rangnick system): vertical football is the attacking idea of going forward quickly, which can also come from a low block (see low-block-counter-attack.json). Popular labels to watch: Dortmund are often called a pure 'pressing' team, but Cox says they mostly used a medium block and rarely a full-pitch press; Bleacher Report says the 'purest' gegenpressing was 2010/11 and that BVB later added containment. A 'Klopp quote on vertical passes' ('much, much greater focus on vertical passes') appeared only in a search summary and was not found on a readable page. Season boundaries 2011/12 and 2012/13 are given as seasons, not dates.
openQuestions: Ids: manager jurgen-klopp (exists); team dortmund-2010-13 (exists, 2010-08-14 to 2013-05-25). No other team/manager ids proposed. Consider as extra exemplars (not researched here): Liverpool 2018-20 is already used by heavy-metal-football; Leicester 2015/16 (Ranieri) and Atletico/Mourinho low-block counters belong to low-block-counter-attack.

Overlap with gegenpressing, heavy-metal-football, red-bull-school: decide whether 'vertical football' is a separate ideology or a facet of them. This file argues it is the attacking/transition-side idea (go forward fast, few passes) not the press; Sky/Cox shows Dortmund counter-pressed 'because Klopp believed it was a valuable attacking tactic'.

The Klopp quote about 'a much, much greater focus on vertical passes' (Vertikalspiel, midway through 2010/11) came only from a search summary; find the primary source (probably Honigstein or Guardian 2011) before using it in statedView.

Bleacher Report page metadata dates (2018) are wrong; texts are from March 2013 (1594218) and about Sept 2013 (1781622, mentions Hamburg 6-2 'earlier in September' i.e. 2013, so its game-management/adaptation claim is after the counted spell end). Dates in sources[] use text-based estimates.

BR2 and Cox disagree on pressing height: BR2 describes all-out gegenpressing, Cox says a medium block and rarely a full-pitch press. Pressing marking: only a 2024 VOOR Sport retrospective places Klopp's counterpressing as space-oriented; no contemporary zonal/man source was read.
Hard Tackle 2012 (Post-Kagawa Trauma) text is mojibake; its claims on Kagawa and Reus were not verified.
Fm-base (tier D) says Dortmund's main aim was 'fast direct passes into the opponents third' - the closest wording to vertical play, but unverifiable.

sources.title: Why Jurgen Klopp's gegenpressing with Dortmund was revolutionary (Sky Sports, Michael Cox book extract)
sources.evidence: It summarised the German obsession with transitions; everyone else loved how Barcelona kept possession, but Klopp studied what they did the moment they lost it.

sources.title: Why Jurgen Klopp's gegenpressing with Dortmund was revolutionary (Sky Sports, Michael Cox book extract)
sources.evidence: Klopp's Dortmund were very different. They were perfectly solid without possession, and defending deep actually suited their counter-attacking. But they gegenpressed because Klopp believed it was a valuable attacking tactic.

sources.title: Why Jurgen Klopp's gegenpressing with Dortmund was revolutionary (Sky Sports, Michael Cox book extract)
sources.evidence: Most typically, Dortmund would use a medium block, standing off the opposition centre-backs, before pressing once the ball was played into the full-backs or midfielders. Dortmund rarely used a full-pitch press, because doing so encouraged the opposition to kick the ball long.

sources.title: Why Jurgen Klopp's gegenpressing with Dortmund was revolutionary (Sky Sports, Michael Cox book extract)
sources.evidence: Klopp's wide midfielders, usually Kevin Grosskreutz and Jakub Blaszczykowski, tucked inside

sources.title: Why Jurgen Klopp's gegenpressing with Dortmund was revolutionary (Sky Sports, Michael Cox book extract)
sources.evidence: Barcelona would recover the ball and then retain possession for long periods, organising themselves in their positional structure.

sources.title: Why Jurgen Klopp's gegenpressing with Dortmund was revolutionary (Sky Sports, Michael Cox book extract)
sources.evidence: If they covered more than 118km collectively in nine out of ten matches, they'd be rewarded with three extra days off during their winter break. The players missed the target, but Klopp generously granted them the extra rest anyway because of their efforts.
sources.note: Anecdote is from Klopp's first season; used as a people-management trait, not 2011-13 behaviour

sources.title: Inside the Tactical Mind of Borussia Dortmund's Juergen Klopp (Bleacher Report)
sources.evidence: BVB's system is to always look for the opportunity to counterattack, playing the ball forward immediately and sprinting into open space as opponents shift from attack to defense.

sources.title: Inside the Tactical Mind of Borussia Dortmund's Juergen Klopp (Bleacher Report)
sources.evidence: Klopp's system was purely one-dimensional, and the risk of all-out attack was that BVB wore little time off the clock when in possession. On an off day for their finishing, Dortmund were vulnerable.

sources.title: Inside the Tactical Mind of Borussia Dortmund's Juergen Klopp (Bleacher Report)
sources.evidence: Dortmund struggle to defend in a classical sense, deep in their own half. And for all their abundant ball-playing class in midfield, they aren't the best at simply maintaining possession and passing the ball around the middle third or playing a containment style of football

sources.title: Inside the Tactical Mind of Borussia Dortmund's Juergen Klopp (Bleacher Report)
sources.evidence: Klopp has since adapted his team's style to include more finesse. Dortmund now cover less ground and, in domestic play, try to take a commanding lead early before taking a foot off the pedal and using more of a containment method.
sources.note: Article written Sept 2013 (after the period); describes adaptation after 2011/12

sources.title: Inside the Tactical Mind of Borussia Dortmund's Juergen Klopp (Bleacher Report)
sources.evidence: Without the ball, there is not much that distinguishes Klopp's gegenpressing from the system Pep Guardiola used at Barcelona, especially in his first season.

sources.title: Tactical Titan: Deconstructing The Kinetics Of Kloppmetry (The Hard Tackle)
sources.evidence: The standard tactics used by Klopp is an attacking 4-2-3-1 with a fast paced pressing game and a high backline.

sources.title: Tactical Titan: Deconstructing The Kinetics Of Kloppmetry (The Hard Tackle)

Kagawa plays the role of an attacking midfielder and provides support for the lone target man, Barrios. The wide players maintain the width. This strategy has a quick counter attacking and direct passing associated with it.
